source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: o1-like reasoning models spend far more tokens than ordinary models on trivial questions. This is the machine version of failing to stop at a good-enough answer.
numbers: On 'what is 2 plus 3', o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models. Tested on QwQ-32B-Preview and DeepSeek-R1 over ASDIV, GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, AIME24.
quote: On average, o1-like models consumed 1,953% more tokens than conventional models
limits: Token counts are the cost measure; no human satisficing baseline.
agent_relevance: Strong case for an S0 gate: easy items should exit early with a short answer.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Most of the extra reasoning comes after the first correct answer. Later solution rounds add little accuracy. The models keep going past a satisfactory option.
numbers: In more than 92% of cases the first solution round was already correct (QwQ: 97% on ASDIV, 93% on MATH500; R1 lower, 89-90%). First round was under 60% of tokens; on ASDIV QwQ first round averaged 287 tokens, 38.7% of the response.
limits: Solutions were split by Llama-3.3-70B, so the split may be noisy. Hard sets (AIME, GPQA) gain more from later rounds.
agent_relevance: A first-correct-then-stop rule (G11, G12) removes about half the tokens on easy items with little loss.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Models produce more solution rounds on easier problems than on harder ones. Effort is mismatched to difficulty.
numbers: QwQ-32B-Preview on ASDIV (easiest) averaged 3.5 solution rounds; fewer on MATH500. Most responses had 2-4 rounds (76-80% of QwQ cases, 59-63% of R1 cases).
limits: Only two model families; difficulty is dataset-level, not item-level.
agent_relevance: A difficulty-scaled effort rule is the opposite of what these models do unaided.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Training the model to stop at its first correct solution (satisficing by training) cuts tokens a lot. Adding one reflection round restores accuracy on hard sets.
numbers: Paper claim: 48.6% fewer tokens with accuracy kept on MATH500. SimPO on shortest responses cut tokens 22.3% on MATH500. QwQ on ASDIV: best method 96.8 accuracy at 2.0 rounds and 381.6 tokens versus 3.5 rounds and 741.8 tokens for the baseline. First-correct-only lowered accuracy on hard MATH500; FCS+Reflection beat it by 1.4 points.
limits: Needs post-training on self-built preference data. Table text was garbled by PDF extraction, so only stated figures are quoted.
agent_relevance: Supports a rule with a check: stop at first pass, but add one verification round on hard items.

source: Liu, Geng, Peterson, Sucholutsky, Griffiths (2025) Large language models assume people are more rational than we really are
finding: Models predicting human gambling choices behave like expected-value maximisers, more than people do. Human choices are bounded; model predictions are not.
numbers: On choices13k (13,000+ gamble problems): correlation with maximum expected value was 0.48 for humans, 0.94 for GPT-4o and 0.93 for GPT-4-Turbo with chain of thought, 0.80 Llama-3-70B, 0.76 Claude 3 Opus, 0.57 Llama-3-8B. Best zero-shot prediction of human choice: GPT-4-Turbo, correlation 0.60, MSE 0.13.
quote: these models deviate from human behavior and align more closely with a classic model of rational choice
limits: Gamble tasks only. Correlation with rational choice rises with capability and with chain of thought.
agent_relevance: Models are poor simulators of bounded agents. Do not use a model to predict how a satisficing user will act without correction.

source: Liu, Geng, Peterson, Sucholutsky, Griffiths (2025) Large language models assume people are more rational than we really are
finding: Chain of thought makes the model more rational, hence less human-like, as a model of choice.
numbers: GPT-4o simulating a human with CoT: correlation 0.90 with expected value, only moderately correlated with human choices. Zero-shot outputs were noisier and less correlated with either.
limits: Prompt effect measured on one dataset.
agent_relevance: Reasoning prompts push toward optimising. Useful for solving, harmful for simulating people.

source: Liu, Geng, Peterson, Sucholutsky, Griffiths (2025) Large language models assume people are more rational than we really are
finding: In the inverse task (infer preferences from observed choices) models match people closely, because people also assume others are rational.
numbers: GPT-4o with CoT: Spearman 0.97 with human inferences (47 observations from Jern et al. 2017). Correlation with rational models: Llama-3-8B CoT 0.62, Llama-3-70B 0.88-0.89, GPT-4o 0.94-0.95.
limits: Small stimulus set of 47 observations.
agent_relevance: Model and human share a belief in rationality, so both can misread a user who takes the first acceptable option.

source: Chen, Liu, Shan, Zhong (2023) The emergence of economic rationality of GPT
finding: GPT passes revealed-preference tests (GARP) better than humans on budget choice tasks. It behaves like a near-perfect optimiser.
numbers: Of 100 GPT runs, 95 (risk), 89 (time), 81 (social), 92 (food) had no GARP violations. Mean CCEI 0.998, 0.997, 0.997, 0.999 versus humans 0.980, 0.985, 0.967, 0.963. GPT higher in every domain (p<0.01, two-sided two-sample t-tests).
limits: Budget-line tasks with numbers, not real-world tasks. CCEI near 1 does not mean human-like preferences.
agent_relevance: Models are not naturally bounded; any satisficing must be imposed by the scaffold.

source: Chen, Liu, Shan, Zhong (2023) The emergence of economic rationality of GPT
finding: Random choice would fail the test, so the high score is not a weak-test artefact.
numbers: 99.9% of simulated random subjects violated GARP.
limits: Power check only.
agent_relevance: Confirms the test can tell optimising from noise.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (PNAS)
finding: GPT-3 shows several human decision biases but not the base-rate fallacy in the taxi problem. It reproduces framing, certainty preference and probability overweighting from prospect theory.
numbers: Replicated Kahneman and Tversky contrasts: framing effect, preference for guaranteed outcomes with slightly lower expected value, and overweighting of 1% vs 2% over 41% vs 42%. Human comparison data from Ruggeri et al.
limits: Text-davinci-002 era model; vignette tasks. The paper warns against over-reading simple behaviour as intelligence.
agent_relevance: Heuristic-like biases come from training text, not bounded resources. A fix by prompt may be needed.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (PNAS)
finding: GPT-3 shows a perseveration bias in a bandit task: it picks the option it has seen more.
numbers: In the information condition where it saw more samples of one option, GPT-3 showed a strong bias to that option even without reason. Authors link it to next-token prediction.
limits: One task, one model.
agent_relevance: Staying with a seen option looks like a satisficing stay but is a copy effect. Test it before relying on it.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2023) Thinking fast and slow in large language models
finding: Older large models answer cognitive reflection test items with the intuitive wrong answer far more often than humans. The newest chat models do not.
numbers: Intuitive-wrong share: GPT-3-davinci family 70-90% versus humans 55%. Correct share: ChatGPT-3.5 59%, ChatGPT-4 96%, GPT-3-davinci-003 5%. Intuitive errors fell to 15% (ChatGPT-3.5) and 0% (GPT-4). 97% of ChatGPT-3.5 and 85% of ChatGPT-4 answers used chain-of-thought. 150 tasks; human control 38% correct versus 41% in the original study.
limits: Conclusion that models lack System 2 is the authors' reading.
agent_relevance: Chain of thought turns the model from fast answerer into deliberator. A gate must decide when this is worth the tokens.

source: Horton, Filippas, Manning (2023) Large language models as simulated economic agents: what can we learn from Homo Silicus?
finding: Proposes using models as simulated economic agents and reruns known behavioural studies, including a framing and status-quo bias scenario, by changing the prompt scenario.
numbers: Reruns a hardware-store price fairness vignette and a status-quo bias study on highway and car safety budgets.
limits: I read the introduction and example outline only; sample sizes not recorded.
agent_relevance: Shows model agents react to framing like humans, so prompt wording matters.

source: Horton et al. (2023) Homo Silicus, methods note
finding: Authors state each simulated agent is a flawed model that may still be useful.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Prompt-dependent.
agent_relevance: Expect results to shift with prompt wording.

source: Binz et al. (2025) Centaur: a foundation model of human cognition
finding: A language model fine-tuned on human choice data (Psych-101) predicts held-out human behaviour better than existing cognitive models and generalises to new tasks.
numbers: Psych-101: 160 experiments, 60,092 participants, 10,681,650 human choices, 253,597,411 text tokens.
limits: I read the abstract and data description only; model-by-model scores not recorded.
agent_relevance: A route to a realistic bounded-user model, if we ever need one.

source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo, Griffiths (2024) Mind your step (by step): chain-of-thought can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse
finding: More deliberation is not always better. On tasks where verbal thinking hurts people, chain of thought also hurts models.
numbers: Implicit statistical learning: CoT drop up to 36.3% absolute (GPT-4o subset 94.00% zero-shot). Another task: GPT-4o 87.50% to 64.40% (drop 23.10%, p<0.0001); Claude 3 Opus 70.70% to 62.70% (8.00%); Gemini 1.5 Pro 68.00% to 61.95% (6.05%); Claude 3.5 Sonnet 65.90% to 67.70% (no significant drop, p=0.969). Learning took up to 331% longer.
limits: Table cells were partly mixed by PDF extraction; model-to-task mapping is approximate. Only some task types (3 of 6) showed drops.
agent_relevance: Supports G1 and S0: reasoning is not free. Gate it by task type.

source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang, Mausam (2023) Let's sample step by step: Adaptive-Consistency
finding: A stopping rule for majority voting: stop drawing samples once agreement is strong enough. This is satisficing on the number of samples.
numbers: Up to 7.9 times fewer samples with an average accuracy drop under 0.1%, over 17 datasets and 3 models. By category: 3.3 times fewer in maths (0.1% drop), 2.9 times commonsense (0.2%), 3.8 times symbolic (no drop), 2.4 times coding. At an average cost of 10 samples, about 3% higher accuracy than plain self-consistency on GSM-8K.
limits: Agreement among samples of one model is not independent evidence (our G4). It saves cost but does not make answers right.
agent_relevance: Template for stopping rules G11/G12: stop on a code-checked agreement threshold, with a hard cap.

source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang, Mausam (2023) Let's sample step by step: Adaptive-Consistency
finding: The stopping criterion is a Beta test on vote counts. Cheap rules (random stop, plain majority, entropy) do worse at equal cost.
numbers: Beta criterion beat Random, Majority and Entropy stopping at equal average sample cost on GSM-8K.
limits: Gains depend on the answer distribution being peaked.
agent_relevance: Use a counted rule, not a model's feeling of being sure.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: iterative refinement with self-feedback
finding: A refine loop with an explicit stopping condition: a set step count, or a stop score from the feedback. Returns diminish by the third pass.
numbers: About 20% absolute average gain over one-step generation (5-40% depending on task). Code optimisation score 22.0 to 28.8 after three iterations; sentiment reversal 33.9 to 36.8; constrained generation 29.0 to 49.7.
quote: The stopping condition stop(f bt, t) either stops at a specified timestep t, or extracts a stopping indicator
limits: Feedback comes from the same model, which G2 and G5 warn about.
agent_relevance: A capped refine loop is fine; use code-checked feedback instead of self-feedback.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts
finding: Search with a threshold and pruning: partial thoughts are rated sure/maybe/impossible and weak ones dropped. A satisficing-style filter on partial solutions.
numbers: Game of 24 with GPT-4: input-output 7.3%, chain of thought 4.0%, CoT self-consistency (k=100) 9.0%, ToT breadth 1: 45%, ToT breadth 5: 74%. Best of 100 chain of thought: 49%.
limits: Needs many model calls; value judgments come from the model itself.
agent_relevance: A cheap threshold lets effort go to promising branches.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters
finding: Allocating test-time compute by prompt difficulty beats uniform spending. Easy prompts need little; hard ones need more.
numbers: Compute-optimal strategy improves efficiency by more than 4x versus a best-of-N baseline. On prompts where a smaller model has non-trivial success, test-time compute can beat a 14x larger model (FLOPs-matched).
limits: Needs a difficulty estimate; gain shrinks on the hardest prompts.
agent_relevance: Core of an effort gate: estimate difficulty, then spend.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large language monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: Coverage grows log-linearly with the number of samples, but picking the right answer is hard without a verifier.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% solved with 1 sample to 56% with 250 samples, above the 43% single-sample best. Without automatic verifiers, common selection methods plateau.
limits: Verifier needed for gains to turn into answers.
agent_relevance: Search until a checker passes (satisfy a test) instead of voting.

source: Sui et al. (2025) Stop overthinking: a survey on efficient reasoning for LLMs
finding: Survey groups efficient-reasoning methods: length rewards, output compression, and prompt-based dynamic routing and budgets.
numbers: Method list includes Token-Budget, SelfBudgeter, ThinkPrune, Plan and Budget, early-exit and sampling-efficient test-time scaling.
limits: I scanned the taxonomy tree, not each method's results.
agent_relevance: A catalogue of stop-early mechanisms to test against our code-checked gate.

source: Sui et al. (2025) Stop overthinking: a survey on efficient reasoning for LLMs
finding: The survey frames overthinking as reasoning that adds length without adding accuracy, matching the satisficing idea of stopping when good enough.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Framing only.
agent_relevance: Use the term overthinking to link our S0 gate to published methods.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts
finding: Plain sampling and refinement without a pruning search stay well below the searched result at similar scale.
numbers: Game of 24, GPT-4: IO + Refine (k=10) 27%; IO best of 100: 33%; CoT best of 100: 49%; ToT breadth 5: 74%.
limits: Compute per method differs; ToT uses more calls per problem.
agent_relevance: Spending samples blindly is worse than spending them on a pruned search with a stop test.
